extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; readers interested in personal/philosophical essays on illness, aging, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern personal essay reflecting on sickness, aging, speech, habits, and conduct; presents practical maxims and reflections rather than formal rules. The text offers behavioral principles (how to speak, how to suffer, how to live) illustrated by examples and classical citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and voice to the matter and the auditor
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak according to the affair you are speaking about to your auditor; the tone and motion of the voice carry expression and meaning and are to be governed by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The voice is not merely to be heard but to 'strike and pierce' — there is a voice to instruct, to flatter, and to reprehend. Example anecdote: one asked to speak softly replied that the speaker must take the tone from the ears of the hearer; Montaigne rejects a purely listener-governed approach and insists the speaker controls tone to convey meaning. Quintilian citation: 'There is a certain voice accommodated to the hearing, not by its loudness, but by its propriety.' Anti-pattern: reducing speech to mere audibility or always lowering voice when told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise patience with illness; avoid impatience
rubrics_metrics.description: We ruin ourselves by impatience; evils (diseases) have their life and limits and should be given their course rather than forcibly cut short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit Nature to take her own way; aggressive attempts to 'cut short' maladies can lengthen and multiply them. Example: Montaigne reports losing some tenacious ailments without help and contrasts excessive medical interference with letting conditions resolve. Scoring note: patience is a practical remedy that often shortens suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow Nature to run its course (therapeutic humility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Nature take her own way; she better understands her own affairs than we do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne favors conceding to natural processes rather than forced medical interventions; he recounts examples where doing 'nothing' shortened ailments. Anti-pattern: aggressive regimens that prolong misery, multiple physicians who keep one in perpetual treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the imagination to lessen suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the imagination gently to assist, flatter, and deceive itself to relieve mental distress caused by illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the disease as ordinary, instructive, or even honorable to obtain consolation (e.g., viewing the stone as 'a noble and dignified disease' that shows strength of mind). Keep a small 'memory book' of past favorable prognostics to counter fear. Anti-pattern: allowing imagination to amplify prognostics and suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anticipatory fear and prognostic anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: He who fears he shall suffer already suffers what he fears; judge by actual sensation, not by fearful reasoning or predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against submitting to doctors' terrifying prognostics; there is great uncertainty in what Nature promises or threatens. Practical rule: monitor present sensations and refrain from feeding fear with hypothetical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe certain ailments as beneficial or instructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Some diseases may be 'medicinal' or provide beneficial reminders—pain can heighten appreciation of health and induce useful reflection toward the end of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the stone can lead to sudden recovery and make health seem more pleasant; diseases can serve to wean one from the world and provide moral instruction. Anti-pattern: seeing every illness only as a catastrophe rather than a possible source of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the necessary mixture of goods and evils in life
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is composed of contrary things; one must know how to make use of them all and to mix them—goods and evils are consubstantial to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to combat natural necessity or to exclude one pole (only sweet tones or only pleasant states) is folly. Use the metaphor of a musician who must employ all tones to play well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on experiential, sensory evidence over abstract medical dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to bodily conditions, the senses inform us sufficiently about what is happening; avoid overreliance on abstruse medical dogmas and alarming prognostications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers simple self-observation to repeated consultations; he keeps notes of symptoms and prior outcomes to ground expectation. Anti-pattern: being swayed by doctors' 'magisterial fopperies' and contradictory prognoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain activity and vigilance throughout life
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity and vigilance are especially recommended to youth and remain central to a life well-lived; life is movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise appropriate to one's capacity: avoid violent exertion in old age but keep moving (walking, riding) to stave off sloth. Montaigne notes he can still ride and walk and that reducing sleep and increasing activity improved his condition. Anti-pattern: long mornings of oversleeping and habitual sloth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice moderation in sleep and meals
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulate sleeping and eating habits; excess sleeping can cause heaviness and disease, and long sittings at table are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne shifted his habits to fewer hours of morning sleep and shorter meals; he tends to sit after others have dined and avoids speaking on a full stomach. Anti-pattern: habitual long sleeps, excessive feasting, and long table-sittings that tire or harm the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity and frugality in upbringing and diet
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave children's formation to common custom and fortune that train them in frugality and hardship; avoid pampering palates and indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises bringing up children modestly (e.g., liking brown bread over sweets) to prevent effeminacy and over-nicety. Diet-wise, he prefers simple preparations, resists delicacies, and disdains curiosity about others' food. Anti-pattern: cultivating pampered tastes and culinary fastidiousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate compassion and assist those most in need
rubrics_metrics.description: Be inclined toward the meaner sort of people; prefer helping those who most need assistance rather than flattering the powerful for gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values solidarity with the needy (example: Cheilonis' loyalty) and criticizes those who flatter the great while neglecting the poor. Moral scoring: favor actions that assist the vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat outward signs with perspective; don't overreact to appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward changes (complexion, face, eyes) often appear worse than they are; friends may pity you before you feel cause; do not be unduly alarmed by the mirror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to bodily signs without letting them dominate the mind; Montaigne notes previous scurvy complexions that proved inconsequential. Anti-pattern: letting external signs trigger panic or unnecessary interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a practical record and learn from past episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain notes of symptoms and past outcomes ('one of paper') to recall favorable prognostics and avoid needless fear when new symptoms arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne compares turning over these notes to consulting the Sibylline leaves to find consolation and precedent. Procedural tip: use past experiential records to temper imagination and expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of elaborate medical remedies that one cannot endure
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether elaborate, violent, or costly cures are worth their misery; some cures bring patients to their graves by their violence or importunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne lists stinking draughts, caustics, incisions, sweats, setons, diets as potentially worse than allowing nature to work; consider cost vs. benefit and the patient's ability to withstand treatment. Anti-pattern: submitting to harsh regimens out of blind trust in medical authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dreams and signs with cautious judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authorities (Plato) advise drawing instruction from dreams, but such interpretations require art and caution; dreams often reflect inclinations rather than reliable prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne is ambivalent: he notes examples of prophetic dreams in authorities but stresses the need for skill to sort and understand them. Practical rule: treat dreams as interesting information, not definitive guidance.
